 The following contains spoilers for Supernatural: Sam Winchester #1, on sale now from Dynamite Entertainment.
 In October 1982, following some sort of acrimony, Cindy Williams left her hit TV sitcom, Laverne and Shirley , and thus the iconic due of Laverne DeFazio and Shirley Feeney was now just...Laverne (the series would still be called Laverne and Shirley for the rest of the season, which proved to be the final one of the show's eight-season run. Amusingly, that season ALSO split up Lenny and Squiggy, Laverne and Shirley's wacky guy friends, for most of the season, as well, as Michael McKean, who played Lenny, was shooting This is Spinal Tap ).

 It was weird seeing Laverne try to get into wacky misadventures by herself, and so, too, is it weird seeing Sam Winchester try to go on adventures without Dean Winchester, but here, at least, it is clear that Sam is being FORCED into these weird adventures!
 Image via Dynamite 
 Supernatural: Sam Winchester #1 is from writer Paulina Ganucheau, artist/colorist Kendall Goode, and letterer Jeff Eckleberry, and it continues the story that originated in Supernatural: Wayward Special #1, where the Winchesters split up because a mysterious entity was threatening Dean's life if Sam didn't agree to so solo apart from his brother (for reasons we still don't understand).
 How Does the Format of the Previous Supernatural Series Set This One Up So Well?
 Image via Dynamite 
 Image via Dynamite 
 Close Image via Dynamite 
 Image via Dynamite 
 The Supernatural series written by Greg Pak that led into this split of the Winchesters was set during the first season of Supernatural , when Dean and Sam were still mostly "just" hunters investigating various supernatural incidents. In other words, before the continuity got REALLY intense for the series.
 The "case of the week" approach made it very simple to fit any number of new stories into that period in time, as we KNOW that Sam and Dean were constantly investigating stuff, so you could very easily say that they had any number of cases outside of the ones shown on the series.
 Not only that, but one of the guiding principles of the early days of the series was just how COMMON all of these incidents were. In other words, we're not talking about a world where the Winchesters uncover every scheme going on. Rather, it was very clear that there were many other problems going on that the Winchesters would NEVER know about, and thus they just handled what they came across in their journeys.
 This is important because it explains how so many evil plots could be uncovered in these stories without really touching on the overall conspiracies that the brothers eventually got caught up in in the series. Thus, that gives Ganucheau a good deal of room to introduce her OWN conspiracy to drive this series, and this series really only works if Ganucheau can come up with a compelling conspiracy that forced Sam to split from his brother.
 Why Is This Time Period So Particularly Well Suited for Sam Being Convinced to Leave Dean?
 Close Image via Dynamite 
 Image via Dynamite 
 Image via Dynamite 
 This story still being set in Season 1 is very important to explain Sam's mindset. Sam, you see, started off the TV series as being NOT part of his family's legacy of "hunting." His brother, Dean, and their father, John, were off hunting while Sam was in college. However, something went terribly wrong to bring him back into the family business.
 Sam's girlfriend (likely soon to be fiancée) Jess was killed by a demon through a horrific process (similar to the one where Dean and Sam's mother was killed), where she was burned alive after being badly wounded. That was heavy on Sam's mind in the early days of the series.
 Therefore, when the mysterious bad guys said that they were going to kill Dean if Sam didn't play ball with them, Sam was in a particularly fragile state of mind for having to lose someone so close to him, and thus he was much more susceptible to this sort of approach (their father, John, was also still alive at this point in the continuity).
 Ganucheau smartly highlights this by adding Dean to Sam's regular nightmares about Jess, and the parallels are explicit. Sam has lost enough, he can't lose his brother, as well.
 I like that Ganucheau also allows for the brothers to continue to communicate, just with Sam making it clear to Dean that they can't work together right now. Dean knows that Sam has been warned to split with him, so he doesn't think that Sam is legitimately wanting to go at it alone, but at the same time, Dean wishes Sam would trust that they can figure this out together.
 Another clever aspect of this series is that Ganucheau is having the mysterious group behind the Dean threats to work as, in effect, Sam's handler now, as he sends Sams on missions to keep Dean safe, while also hopefully doing SOME good in the process, as well.
 If I had a concern about the opening of the series, it would be that we didn't learn quite that much about the case that Sam is investigating. The first issue ends on a cliffhanger before too much is explained, and I think that things might have been better served by learning more about the mystery in the series.
 Kendall Goode is a fine sequential storyteller. I don't know if I necessarily love this particular art style on Sam's supernatural adventures, but it is evident that the storytelling of the series helps Ganucheau a lot, as Goode can do a nice job bringing Ganucheau's ideas to life in a cohesive fashion.
 The issue had a nice cliffhanger to it. The stories that the Winchesters get into are rarely ones that are suitable for children, so seeing a story that INVOLVES a young person was a clever way of getting around that established limitation.
